true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently overrides the 4-argument version

Two class methods named `downsize` are defined: one with signature `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` (lines 145-147) and immediately after another with signature `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` (lines 149-151). In Ruby the second definition completely replaces the first, so the 4-positional-argument form is dead code and no longer callable. Any existing caller elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. thumbnail generation code) that still calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, width, height, opts)` will now raise an ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments) because the method only accepts 2 positional args plus opts. This is a breaking API change that is easy to miss since Ruby only emits a silent 'method redefined' warning.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB upload size replaces configurable site settings

`validateUploadedFile` used to read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, allowing admins to configure separate size limits for images vs. attachments. It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` KB for all upload types, so the `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb` site settings are silently ignored on the client side. This creates an inconsistency with the server, which still reads `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` in `uploads_controller.rb` for the new downsizing feature, meaning client-side validation no longer matches server-side behavior for sites that configure a limit different from 10MB.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB download cap for API URL uploads ignores max_image_size_kb setting

`FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` was changed to `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. This removes respect for the admin-configured `max_image_size_kb` setting when downloading images via API URL, allowing files up to 10MB regardless of the configured limit. While the new downsizing logic will later try to shrink the file, this silently changes the download-time cap for all sites, including those that intentionally set a stricter limit, and is inconsistent with the rest of the codebase which still references `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` elsewhere (e.g. `migrate_to_new_scheme`).

Hardcoded 10MB value in displayErrorForUpload loses configured max_image_size_kb

`displayErrorForUpload` previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` to show the correct configured limit in the 413 error message. It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` KB, so the error message shown to users will be wrong whenever an admin configures a different `max_image_size_kb` value, misleading users about the actual upload limit.

In-place downsizing writes output over the same file being read, risking corruption

The downsizing loop calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)`, using the same path for both source and destination. Image tools such as ImageMagick's `convert` and `gifsicle` are not guaranteed to be safe when input and output paths are identical — depending on how they open/truncate the output file, this can corrupt or truncate the file mid-read, especially for multi-frame/animated GIFs processed via gifsicle. This can result in a corrupted or zero-byte image being uploaded instead of a properly downsized one, with no validation afterward to catch this failure mode.

No tests added for new automatic downsizing behavior

The PR introduces non-trivial new logic (retry loop with a hardcoded attempt limit, size comparisons, and reliance on `OptimizedImage.downsize`) in `create_upload`, as well as a signature change in `OptimizedImage.downsize`/`optimize`. No spec changes are included to cover the new downsizing loop (e.g., verifying it stops after reaching the limit, after exhausting attempts, or that it is skipped for non-image uploads), leaving this feature and the related method signature change unverified by automated tests.

Return value of OptimizedImage.downsize is ignored, allowing silent failures and oversized uploads

The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(...)` but never checks its boolean return value (it returns false on failure, e.g. ImageMagick exits non-zero). If downsizing fails, the loop will burn through all 5 attempts without reducing size and the code falls through to `Upload.create_for` and uploads a file that still exceeds `max_image_size_kb`, with no error reported to the user or logged specifically for this scenario, defeating the purpose of the size limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation callback crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil

`self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` and the following `sub!` are called unconditionally in `before_validation`, without checking whether `host` is nil. If `host` is nil (e.g. the `embeddable_host` param key is missing in the admin controller, or `EmbeddableHost.new` is used without setting host first), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil:NilClass` instead of producing a normal validation error, resulting in an unhandled 500 error rather than a controlled validation failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy raise NoMethodError (500) instead of 404 for unknown host id

`host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` returns `nil` when the id doesn't exist. In `update`, `save_host(nil)` then calls `host.host = ...` on nil, raising NoMethodError. In `destroy` (line 15-16), `host.destroy` is called on a potentially nil object with the same result. Both actions will produce an unhandled 500 error instead of a proper 404/`render_json_error` response for a missing record.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped string interpolation into raw SQL INSERT during migration

`execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"` interpolates the `h` value (parsed from the pre-existing `embeddable_hosts` site setting) directly into SQL without escaping. If any historical host value contains a single quote or other SQL metacharacter, this migration will fail or behave unexpectedly. The migration should use parameterized execution (e.g., `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote`) instead of raw interpolation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when no category matches the embed_category setting (the common/default case)

`category_id = execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i` assumes the query returns at least one row. Since `embed_category` previously defaulted to an empty string and most installs never set a category whose name equals the setting's raw value, this query will typically return zero rows. Indexing an empty PG::Result with `[0]` yields `nil`, and calling `['id']` on `nil` raises `NoMethodError`, aborting the migration for essentially every existing installation that hasn't explicitly matched a category name to the `embed_category` setting value. This blocks upgrades rather than falling through to the `uncategorized_category_id` fallback that follows.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

false_positives.candidate:
Client-side category badge can diverge from server-assigned category when none is chosen

After `host.save(props)` succeeds, the component does `host.set('category', Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')))`. If no category was selected (`categoryId` is null), this sets `category` to `undefined`, while the server (`Admin::EmbeddableHostsController#save_host`) falls back to `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id` for blank category_id. This leaves the UI showing no/blank category badge even though the host was actually persisted with the uncategorized category, until a full page reload re-fetches the correct data.

No behavioral test coverage for create/update/destroy of embeddable hosts

This spec only asserts that `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. There is no test exercising `create`, `update`, or `destroy`, no test for validation failures, no test for the not-found path (which, per the controller bug, currently 500s), and no test confirming staff-only access is enforced in practice. Given this controller manages the whitelist of hosts allowed to embed content (a security-sensitive feature), the lack of functional test coverage is a significant gap.

No behavioral test coverage for the embedding show/update actions

This spec, like the embeddable_hosts_controller spec, only checks the class hierarchy. There's no test verifying `show` or `update` actually renders the expected serialized `embedding` payload containing `embeddable_hosts`, nor any check of the `fetch_embedding` before_filter behavior.

No pretender mocks added for the new admin embedding endpoints

This PR adds new client-side adapters/controllers/routes/components for managing embeddable hosts (`GET/PUT /admin/customize/embedding`, `POST/PUT/DELETE /admin/embeddable_hosts`), but no corresponding mock endpoints were added to the test pretender, and no new JS test files were added to exercise the admin-embedding route/controller/component. This leaves the entire new admin UI feature without JS test coverage.

Plural `_ids` hydration doesn't guard against failed subtype lookups

In the new pluralized branch of `_hydrateEmbedded`, `obj[k].map(id => self._lookupSubType(subType, type, id, root))` is assigned directly to `obj[self.pluralize(subType)]` without filtering out `undefined` results, unlike the singular branch which only assigns when `hydrated` is truthy. If any id in the `_ids` array doesn't resolve to an object in the root payload's corresponding collection (e.g. a `color_ids` entry not present in the sideloaded `colors` array), the resulting array will contain `undefined` entries, which can cause runtime errors when templates/components call `.get()` on those entries.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unhandled nil TopicUser causes 500 error in unsubscribe action

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (e.g. a user who navigates directly to the unsubscribe URL for a topic they were never notified about or that never created a topic_user row). The following lines immediately call `tu.notification_level` and `tu.save!` without a nil check, which will raise `NoMethodError` and produce an unhandled 500 error instead of a graceful response.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Misspelled property name 'stopNotificiationsText'

The computed property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (missing an 'a', should be `stopNotificationsText`). It's used consistently in the matching template (`{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}`) so it functions, but the typo will confuse future maintainers and complicate searching/refactoring this code.

false_positives.candidate:
No controller specs added for the new unsubscribe action

The PR introduces a new `TopicsController#unsubscribe` action with non-trivial branching logic (slug mismatch redirect, notification level toggling between muted/regular/tracking/watching, nil-handling risk noted separately), and a new `Topic#unsubscribe_url` helper, but no new or updated controller/model specs were added to verify this behavior (e.g. correct notification level transitions, redirect behavior on slug mismatch, response format handling).

No test coverage verifying the unsubscribe_url is actually rendered in the email

The test fixture `message_with_unsubscribe` now passes `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"`, but none of the existing assertions check that this URL is actually interpolated into the rendered `unsubscribe_link` text/body/html_part. The only assertion reused (`has the user preferences url in the body`) predates this change and does not exercise the new per-topic unsubscribe link behavior, so a regression in the `%{unsubscribe_url}` interpolation (e.g. missing argument errors, or the URL simply not appearing) would not be caught by this spec.

State-changing action exposed via GET request (CSRF exposure) The `unsubscribe` action mutates persistent state (changes `TopicUser#notification_level`) but is routed as a GET endpoint (`config/routes.rb`: `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe" => "topics#unsubscribe"`). Rails' CSRF protection by default only guards unsafe (non-GET) verbs, so this endpoint is not covered by CSRF tokens. Any third party page can trigger this mutation for a logged-in user simply by causing their browser to issue a GET to this URL (e.g. via an `` tag, link prefetching, or crawler), silently changing/muting their topic notification settings without consent.

Template path inconsistent with flat route/controller naming, may fail to resolve

The new route is registered with a flat name `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', ...)` in app-route-map.js.es6, and its controller/view are placed using the matching flat naming convention (`controllers/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, `views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`). However the template was placed in a nested path `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` instead of the flat `templates/topic-unsubscribe.hbs`. Under the classic Ember resolver conventions used elsewhere in this codebase, a flat route name resolves to a flat (dasherized) template name, not a nested directory path. This mismatch risks the template not being found/resolved for the `topicUnsubscribe` route, resulting in a blank or broken unsubscribe page.

unsubscribe_link translation now requires unsubscribe_url but is not validated

`config/locales/server.en.yml`'s `unsubscribe_link` string was changed to embed `%{unsubscribe_url}`, and `MessageBuilder#html_part`/`#body` render it via `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `@opts[:add_unsubscribe_link]` is true. There is no guard ensuring `unsubscribe_url` is present in `template_args` for every caller that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true`. Any current or future caller (mailer or plugin) that enables `add_unsubscribe_link` without supplying `unsubscribe_url` will raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` at email-build time, breaking that notification entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Email validation (and its side effects) runs twice per signup, double-counting blocked-email statistics

In `create`, `user.valid?` is called first (left operand of `&&`, so it always executes regardless of `call_discourse_hub?`), and later `user.save` triggers the full validation chain again. Because `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which has the side effect of incrementing `match_count` and updating `last_match_at` on every invocation, a single signup attempt against a blocked email will increment the counter twice instead of once, corrupting the abuse statistics the feature is meant to produce.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked email matching is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass

BlockedEmail.should_block? queries `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` using the raw email string exactly as submitted by the user, with no downcasing/normalization. Since the User model does not appear to normalize/downcase the email before validation runs (normalization such as Email.downcase is only used elsewhere, e.g. find_by_username_or_email), an attacker can trivially bypass a block entry such as 'spam@evil.com' by signing up with 'Spam@Evil.com' or any different casing. This defeats the entire purpose of the blocked-email feature.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
No test coverage for the migrated whitelist/blacklist domain validation logic

The whitelist/blacklist domain-restriction logic (`email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist`) was moved out of User#email_validator into this new EmailValidator class, but spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb only exercises the new 'blocked email' branch (lines 9-21) via stubbed BlockedEmail.should_block?. There is no test verifying that the whitelist/blacklist branches still add the `not_allowed` error correctly after being refactored into this class, so a regression in that previously-tested behavior would go unnoticed.

Structured per-field errors and submitted values now exposed on signup failure, enabling account/field enumeration

The `create` action's failure response now includes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` in addition to the message. Previously only a combined message string was returned. Returning a machine-readable mapping of which specific field failed (e.g. `errors: {email: ["has already been taken"]}`) makes it trivial for an automated script to enumerate which emails/usernames are already registered or blocked, which is a stronger enumeration primitive than the prior free-text message.

rejectedEmails permanently blacklists an email for any email-related server error, not just blocked/invalid emails

In createAccount's failure handler, any response where `result.errors.email` is present causes `result.values.email` to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` forever (for the life of the controller instance), regardless of the actual reason for the email error (blocked email, domain restriction, transient server/DiscourseHub failure, etc.). Once added, `emailValidation` will always report that email as failed even if the underlying condition was transient or already resolved (e.g. a temporary DiscourseHub timeout), preventing the user from ever resubmitting that same email in the same session without reloading the page.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses unsafe substring match

`postMessageReceived` validates the sender using `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, i.e. it checks whether the message's origin string appears anywhere inside `discourseUrl`, rather than checking that `e.origin` equals (or is a prefix match of) the trusted Discourse origin. This is a well-known postMessage anti-pattern: a crafted or coincidental origin that happens to be a substring of `discourseUrl` (e.g. a shared domain fragment) could pass this check and have its `discourse-resize` messages accepted, allowing an untrusted page to manipulate the iframe height from outside the embed context.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Potential NoMethodError when RSS/Atom item has no content

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes `i.content` is always present. Many RSS 2.0 feeds use `description` rather than `content`, and SimpleRSS will return `nil` for a missing `content` field, causing `.scrub` to raise `NoMethodError` on `nil` and aborting the whole feed-polling job (and since `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the failure is silently dropped) for every item that lacks a `content` element, not just the problematic one.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Core poll_feed RSS parsing/import logic is untested

The spec only verifies that `execute` delegates to `poll_feed` under the right site-setting conditions, but it never exercises `poll_feed` itself: there is no coverage for RSS/Atom item iteration, URL fallback to `i.id`, HTML unescaping, or the call to `TopicEmbed.import`. Given this is the main new behavior introduced by this PR (feed-based topic creation/import), the lack of a test for `poll_feed`'s actual body is a significant gap.

Full feed poll executed synchronously per missing embed request

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline whenever an embed_url isn't found and feed polling is enabled, which downloads and parses the entire configured RSS/Atom feed and imports every item just to possibly locate the single requested embed_url. Because the throttle in `retrieved_recently?` is keyed per `embed_url`, concurrent requests for different not-yet-imported embed URLs each trigger their own full feed fetch/parse/import cycle with no global throttle, which can hammer the external feed URL and do redundant work under load (e.g. many visitors loading many different not-yet-cached embed pages at once).

New gems only reflected in the Rails 4 lockfile

The Gemfile adds `ruby-readability` and `simple-rss` unconditionally (outside the rails3/rails4 branch), but only `Gemfile_rails4.lock` is updated in this diff to include them. The repository supports dual-booting Rails 3 via a separate default `Gemfile.lock` (per the monkey-patching at the top of the Gemfile); if that lockfile isn't also updated, `bundle install`/`bundle exec` in Rails 3 mode will fail or be inconsistent with the new dependencies required by the embed/feed-import feature.

Protocol-relative URLs are mangled by absolutize_urls

`absolutize_urls` treats any href/src starting with '/' as a site-relative URL and rewrites it by stripping all leading slashes and prefixing with the embed site's scheme+host. Protocol-relative URLs such as `//cdn.example.com/x.jpg` also start with '/', so this code strips both leading slashes and produces `http://<embedhost>/cdn.example.com/x.jpg` instead of leaving the external URL `http://cdn.example.com/x.jpg` untouched. This breaks images/links that use protocol-relative URLs, which are common on syndicated content.

Referer host comparison is case-sensitive

`URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host` compares hostnames with case-sensitive string equality. Hostnames are case-insensitive, so a referer like `Example.com` would fail to match a configured `embeddable_host` of `example.com` (or vice versa), causing legitimate embed requests to be incorrectly rejected with InvalidAccess.

feed_key is defined but never used

`feed_key` computes a Redis cache key presumably meant to track the feed's last-modified state (to avoid reprocessing/refetching unchanged feeds), but it is never referenced anywhere in `poll_feed`. As written, the job always re-downloads and re-parses the entire feed and iterates every item on every run, with no last-modified/ETag based short-circuiting, making this dead code and a missed optimization opportunity.

raw_html cook_method bypasses all sanitization for externally sourced content

Post#cook now returns `raw` unmodified when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, completely skipping PrettyText/post_analyzer rendering and sanitization. This path is used by TopicEmbed.import for content retrieved from RSS feeds and third-party web pages via Readability (app/models/topic_embed.rb). Since the content originates from an untrusted external source (a feed the admin configured, or any page fetched via the embed flow), and the resulting `cooked` HTML is rendered unescaped (`<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb and in normal topic views), a malicious or compromised feed/page can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes in the context of the forum for every visitor who views that topic, not just inside the embed iframe. This is a stored XSS vector that defeats the forum's normal sanitization guarantees.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Mixing float with flexbox children breaks layout of .small-action

`.small-action` was converted to a flex container (`@include flexbox(); @include align-items(center);`), but its direct children `.topic-avatar` (line ~270, `float: left;`) and `button` (line ~309, `float: right;`) still rely on `float`. In CSS, `float` is ignored on flex items (direct children of a `display:flex` container). As a result the avatar will no longer be positioned via float but will simply become the first flex item (which happens to look similar), while the `button`'s `float: right` will have no effect at all — it will just be laid out as the last flex item in normal flow instead of being pushed to the right edge of the container. This silently breaks the right-alignment of the action button (e.g. undo/dismiss controls on small-action notices) without any compensating `margin-left: auto` or `justify-content` change. The trailing `clear: both;` on `.small-action` is also now vestigial since there are no floated children to clear within the flex container.

Removed `.badge-wrapper.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` inside `.extra-info-wrapper` without equivalent replacement

The previous rule gave bullet-style badge wrappers inside `.extra-info-wrapper` a 5px top margin for vertical alignment. This specific rule was deleted and replaced only with a `line-height: 1.5` on the parent `.extra-info-wrapper`. Line-height alone does not reproduce a per-element top margin; depending on surrounding content this can cause the bullet badge to misalign vertically relative to the rest of the extra-info row, since the compensating offset for the bullet variant is gone.

Removed `.title { float: left; }` rule without replacement when converting `.contents` to flexbox

The diff removes the `.title { float: left; }` rule nested inside `.d-header .contents` while turning `.contents` into a flex container. No `order` or other flex-specific rule was added for `.title` to replace the old floating behavior, unlike `.panel` which received `margin-left: auto; @include order(3);`. If `.title` is one of the flex items inside `.contents`, its layout now depends entirely on flex default behavior (order 0, normal flex-basis) with no explicit styling, which may differ from the previous floated layout and could shift or resize the site title/logo area unexpectedly.

`@include order(2)` added to `.extra-info-wrapper` with no visible flex container context

`.extra-info-wrapper` now has `@include order(2)` applied, but the CSS `order` property only has an effect on elements that are direct children of a flex (or grid) container. Nothing in this file establishes `.extra-info-wrapper`'s parent as `display: flex`. I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! (added in set_locale) is the only place that forces the whole fallback chain (current locale, site default locale, :en) to be loaded via I18n.ensure_loaded!. Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of one-way hash

Backup codes are encrypted with symmetricEncrypt/symmetricDecrypt using CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY (see also setup.ts line 68), the same way the TOTP secret is stored. Unlike the TOTP secret, backup codes never need to be recovered in plaintext for comparison — they only need equality checking, so they should be hashed with a one-way function (e.g. bcrypt/argon2) like passwords. Storing them with reversible encryption means that if CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is ever compromised, every user's full set of backup/recovery codes can be recovered in plaintext, defeating the purpose of a second factor recovery mechanism.

Missing `prisma` import causes compile/runtime failure in Salesforce CalendarService

The new `getClient` method calls `await prisma.credential.update({...})`, but the file never imports `prisma` (e.g. `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`). This is a plain reference error that should fail TypeScript type-checking and will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime, breaking every Salesforce calendar operation (create/update/delete event, availability) since `getClient` is invoked unconditionally from the constructor.

No automated tests for the new credential-sync webhook or OAuth refresh/credential utilities

The PR adds a new, security-sensitive webhook endpoint (`app-credential.ts`) plus shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`) that affect token refresh for ~10 apps, but ships with no unit or integration tests (the author explicitly checked 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective'). Given the response-shape bugs identified in refreshOAuthTokens consumers, tests covering both the sync-enabled and sync-disabled code paths would have caught these regressions before merge.

Salesforce access token is refreshed on every CalendarService instantiation with no expiry check

Unlike other providers (hubspot, zoho-bigin, zohocrm, office365, zoomvideo, webex), the new Salesforce `getClient` unconditionally POSTs to Salesforce's OAuth token endpoint every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, regardless of whether the current access token is still valid. There is no `isTokenValid`/expiry check guarding the refresh call. This causes unnecessary refresh-token round trips on every booking operation, risking rate limiting and unnecessary rotation of refresh tokens (some OAuth providers invalidate the previous refresh token on each refresh, which under concurrent requests could cause race conditions where one request's refresh token becomes stale before it is persisted). Additionally, this refresh call does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so Salesforce credential syncing (the stated purpose of this PR) is not actually wired up for this app despite other apps being updated.

parseRefreshTokenResponse now throws unconditionally on invalid tokens, changing previously tolerant error handling in Office365

Previously, office365calendar's refresh flow used `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(responseJson)` directly and, on failure, logged the Zod error plus the raw MS response and continued gracefully (merging only successfully-parsed fields, keeping the stale credentials). The new shared `parseRefreshTokenResponse` helper throws an `Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` whenever parsing fails, and the office365 diagnostic `console.error` logging of the zod error / MS response was removed. This changes office365's refresh behavior from a soft, loggable failure to a hard throw, and removes debugging visibility into why Microsoft's token response failed validation — a regression for an existing, unrelated code path incidental to this feature.

symmetricDecrypt call is not wrapped in try/catch

`symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...)` followed by `JSON.parse(...)` can throw if the payload is malformed or was encrypted with a different key. There is no try/catch around this, so a bad request results in an unhandled exception / generic 500 instead of a clear validation error, making it harder for self-hosters to diagnose integration issues with their own sync service.

Using Prisma's atomic `{ retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` would avoid this race and ensure the failure count is accurate, which matters since after retryCount > 1 the reminder is permanently deleted.

This PR adds a materially new and fairly intricate cancellation flow (cancelled flag set at cancel/reschedule time, consumed by this CRON job up to 1 hour before scheduledDate, interacting with SendGrid's scheduled_sends API) specifically to fix a production bug where reminders for cancelled/rescheduled bookings were still sent. When rescheduling, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` is called with `immediateDelete=true`, which synchronously calls SendGrid's cancel endpoint right away instead of marking the reminder `cancelled: true` for the throttled CRON-based cancellation introduced by this PR. The PR's stated rationale is that direct/immediate SendGrid cancellations build up against SendGrid's max of 100 pending cancellations and start failing silently, causing reminders to still be sent. By using `immediateDelete=true` here, bulk/rapid rescheduling (e.g. for recurring events or round-robin events) can reintroduce exactly that failure mode for the reschedule flow, even though the booking-cancellation flow (handleCancelBooking.ts) was fixed to defer via the `cancelled` flag.

SMS reminder DB row is only deleted if twilio.cancelSMS succeeds, unlike previous unconditional deletion

Previously, callers (e.g. handleCancelBooking.ts) unconditionally ran `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` for every reminder regardless of whether the external cancellation call succeeded. Now `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` performs `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` inside the same try block; if `twilio.cancelSMS` throws (e.g. invalid/expired SID, Twilio API error), the subsequent delete is skipped and the error is swallowed by the catch block (just logged). The for-loop that cancels pending email reminders (lines 56-73) is wrapped in a single try/catch around the whole loop. If `client.request` throws for any one reminder (e.g. an invalid/expired batch_id), the loop stops immediately: (1) all subsequent reminders in `remindersToCancel` are skipped for this cron run even though their scheduledDate may be within the next hour, meaning their emails can still be sent — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix; (2) `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` calls created for reminders that WERE successfully cancelled earlier in the loop are Prisma 'thenable' lazy promises that only execute when awaited via `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)`. In the `delete` mutation, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` is called for every scheduled reminder belonging to a deleted workflow. false_positives.candidate:
No test exercises strategy close()/recreate across a simulated rebalance

All of the new thread-queue-parallel tests (test_thread_queue_parallel, test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order, etc.) build a single strategy via factory.create_with_partitions() and only ever call factory.shutdown() at the end; none of them call consumer.close() (or terminate()) and then call factory.create_with_partitions() again to simulate a Kafka rebalance and continue processing more messages. This is exactly the scenario where the shared FixedQueuePool gets torn down by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() (see related finding), so the test suite does not catch that the thread-queue-parallel mode becomes non-functional after the first rebalance.

Queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates each worker queue as queue.Queue() with no maxsize (line 185), yet the class docstring (around line 253, 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up') and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring both claim backpressure is provided. Because the queues are unbounded, a single slow/stuck group can cause its queue to grow without limit while submit() keeps accepting and enqueuing new items, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the advertised backpressure. This undermines the stated goal of isolating a slow item's impact.

Relies on Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API

queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added in Python 3.13. OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132-133, 142-143) and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) (line 238) to unblock worker threads. If the project's supported/runtime Python version is older than 3.13, q.shutdown() will raise AttributeError (caught and merely logged at line 238-240), but the workers will then never receive a ShutDown signal and will remain blocked forever on work_queue.get(), so worker.join(timeout=5.0) will always time out without the thread actually stopping. This silently defeats the entire graceful-shutdown mechanism on any Python version prior to 3.13.

Sequential worker joins in shutdown() can block for minutes

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 231-243) iterates over all workers sequentially and calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) for each one. With the default num_queues=20, if several workers are slow to exit (e.g. stuck in a long-running result_processor call), the overall shutdown can block for up to num_queues * 5 seconds (100s by default) before returning. Combined with the fact that this shutdown path is invoked from strategy close()/terminate() on every rebalance (see related finding), this can cause the whole consumer to stall far beyond typical graceful-shutdown/rebalance timeouts, risking forced kills by orchestration and loss of the ability to commit final offsets.

close()/terminate() tear down the shared, persistent FixedQueuePool, breaking processing after any rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (line 335-338) and terminate() (line 340-342) both call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently stops all worker threads and shuts down all underlying queue.Queue objects. However, queue_pool is the SAME object that lives on ResultsStrategyFactory (created once in __init__, see result_consumer.py) and is intended to persist across the whole lifetime of the consumer process - it is only supposed to be torn down once via ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(). In Arroyo, create_with_partitions() is invoked on every partition assignment change (rebalance), and the previous strategy instance's close()/join() are called first. That means on the very first rebalance, the shared queue_pool's workers/queues are shut down for good, while factory.queue_pool still points at this now-dead pool. The next strategy created by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker() reuses this dead queue_pool. When submit() then calls work_queue.put(work_item) on a queue that has been shut down, queue.ShutDown is raised, caught by the broad except Exception in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), which force-marks the offset as added+completed without ever having it processed. The net effect: after the first rebalance, uptime results stop being processed entirely while Kafka offsets keep advancing normally (silent data loss, no lag/alerting signal).

get_committable_offsets does an O(n) scan under a lock on every tick, scaling with backlog size

get_committable_offsets() (lines 67-98) iterates offset-by-offset from last_committed+1 to max_offset while holding the per-partition lock, and this runs every second from the commit loop. If one group backlogs its queue (the exact scenario this PR intends to tolerate), the gap between last_committed and max_offset for that partition grows large, making this scan increasingly expensive and holding the partition lock longer each tick - which blocks add_offset()/complete_offset() calls from worker threads processing unrelated groups on the same partition, partially reintroducing the contention the queue-based design was meant to avoid.

join(timeout) ignores the caller-supplied timeout

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) (lines 344-345) ignores the timeout parameter entirely and always calls self.close(), which itself uses hardcoded internal timeouts (5.0s for the commit thread plus up to 5.0s per worker in queue_pool.shutdown()). Callers (e.g. Arroyo's StreamProcessor, which is configured with join_timeout) expect join() to respect the requested deadline for bounding shutdown time; ignoring it can make the strategy's shutdown take substantially longer than what was configured, breaking the ProcessingStrategy contract.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache key can collide across distinct (name, parentFolder) pairs

userPermDenialCacheKey builds the cache key by naively concatenating userUID, action, name and parent with '_' as separator: namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. Because resource UIDs (name/parentFolder) can themselves legally contain underscores, two different requests can produce the same concatenated string, e.g. name="ab_cd", parent="ef" and name="ab", parent="cd_ef" both yield "..._ab_cd_ef". When this happens, a denial cached for one (name, parent) pair will be served for an unrelated resource, causing an incorrect 'denied' result to be returned for a resource the caller actually has access to (or, if the collision is reversed, the opposite type of mistake could occur with other callers sharing the key space). This is a correctness/security risk introduced by the new denial cache, since the previous caches never combined multiple variable-length, potentially-overlapping fields into one key this way.

For code paths that perform many individual Check calls in a loop (e.g., per-item authorization checks), this removes a previously-available fast path and could noticeably increase per-request latency/CPU, even though the server now has its own cache, because the gRPC call overhead itself is no longer avoided on repeated checks within the same request.
