No test added verifying SQL expressions are blocked regardless of feature toggle state

This PR is a security fix meant to permanently disable SQL Expressions (to close an RCE/LFI vulnerability), but no test was added to pkg/expr covering ReadQuery with QueryTypeSQL for both FlagSqlExpressions enabled and disabled, asserting that an error is always returned. Given the severity of the vulnerability being fixed and the confusing logic in enableSqlExpressions, a regression test is necessary to prevent this security control from being accidentally removed or inverted in a future change.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the full-function lock in BuildIndex allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu.Lock() for its entire duration, which incidentally serialized all builds, including two concurrent calls for the same NamespacedResource key. The new code only takes cacheMu when writing the final result into b.cache (near the end of the function), so two goroutines can now run BuildIndex concurrently for the same key (this is a real possibility because searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex in search.go checks GetIndex and calls build() without any per-key lock, a gap already flagged by a TODO comment in that file). Concurrent builds for the same key can both call bleve.New()/bleve.NewMemOnly() and write documents independently, then race to overwrite b.cache[key], silently discarding one index's work or, for file-backed indexes sharing the same directory, causing on-disk index corruption/contention.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs() reads the cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache directly without acquiring cacheMu (not even RLock), while BuildIndex now performs genuinely concurrent writes to b.cache under its own lock (enabled by the finer-grained locking introduced in this PR, combined with the worker pool in searchSupport.init that builds multiple namespaces in parallel). Because real concurrent map writes now happen during startup/runtime, a concurrent call to TotalDocs() (e.g. from a metrics scrape or another caller) racing with a BuildIndex write to the same map can trigger Go's 'concurrent map read and map write' fatal error, crashing the process. This hazard existed before but is made materially worse by the increased real concurrency this PR introduces for cache writes.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer now blocks synchronously on full index build during startup

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) directly in the constructor, which in turn calls searchSupport.init(), which builds the search index for every namespace returned by GetResourceStats before returning. Previously this cost was paid lazily inside the first gRPC call (with its own deadline); now it is paid unconditionally at construction time with no timeout. If NewResourceServer is invoked anywhere besides the dedicated storage-server module (e.g. during normal Grafana app-server bootstrap for unified storage), overall process startup can block for an arbitrarily long time while every namespace's index is built, and any failure during that build (e.g. a transient DB error) now causes server construction itself to fail outright rather than only a particular RPC. The PR description explicitly raises this as an open question ('What could this break?') but does not resolve it — there is no bound on index-build time nor any fallback/async option.

Postgres integration test disabled instead of fixed, losing coverage for the exact startup-init change

This PR adds a skip for dbType == "postgres" in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer with only the comment 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' No root cause or follow-up ticket is referenced. Since this PR's core change is moving unified-storage initialization into server startup (which can now block or fail at NewResourceServer time), disabling exactly the integration test that exercises a real storage-server startup against postgres removes the only regression coverage for that scenario, rather than investigating why it fails under the new init-at-startup behavior.

Stop() no longer gates any RPC after shutdown

Previously every RPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) called s.Init(ctx) first; since Init used sync.Once, after Stop() set s.initErr to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", those calls to Init(ctx) would surface that error to callers. This PR removes the s.Init(ctx) calls from all RPC handlers, so the initErr set in Stop() is now write-only dead state — no code path reads it anymore. As a result, after Stop() is called, in-flight or new RPCs will no longer get a clean 'service is stopping/stopped' error; they will instead proceed against a server whose background context (s.ctx) has already been cancelled (e.g. broadcaster/watch loops torn down), leading to inconsistent or silent failures instead of a clear error to the caller.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup uses a hard-coded wrong alias, so created IdPs are never removed

In the new testCacheIDPForLogin test, cleanups are registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` (lines 381 and 425), using the literal string "alias" instead of the actual alias that was just created (e.g. "idp-alias-" + i, or "idp-alias-20"). As a result, the cleanup callback attempts to delete a non-existent identity provider named "alias" instead of the ones created by the test, so the 20+ identity providers created in this test are never actually removed after the test runs. This can leak test data across test executions/tests in the suite (the same organization "orga"/"orgb" are reused by other tests in this class) and may also cause cleanup-time failures (404 on delete) that mask the real test result.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
remove() now unconditionally calls the backend delegate, defeating the cache

In remove(String alias), `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is now executed unconditionally before checking cache validity. Previously, the delegate (JPA) lookup only happened when `isInvalid(cacheKey)` was true; when the cache entry was valid, the code used the already-cached `CachedIdentityProvider` via `realmCache.getCache().get(cacheKey, ...)` without hitting the backend. With this change, every call to remove() now performs an extra backend lookup even in the common case where the idp is already cached and valid, which is a performance regression that partially defeats the purpose of this caching layer. The fetched `storedIdp` is only actually needed for the `registerIDPLoginInvalidation` call and for the (already-existing) invalid-cache branch; it should be computed lazily/only when needed instead of unconditionally up front.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() does not actually return the BouncyCastle provider

The CryptoProvider interface documents getBouncyCastleProvider() as returning the BouncyCastle (or FIPS) security provider. This implementation instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), i.e. whatever provider happens to back the JVM's default keystore type (e.g. the SUN or PKCS12 provider), which has nothing to do with BouncyCastle. Any caller that relies on this method to obtain the actual BC provider (e.g. to reference its name or algorithms) will get a misleading/incorrect result when this is the active CryptoProvider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code creates and discards ASN1Encoder instances

In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` construct encoders, write into them, and then discard the result without using it anywhere. This is leftover/dead code that wastes cycles and allocations on every signature conversion and should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

false_positives.candidate:
New mandatory CryptoIntegration.init() call changes AuthzClient.create() behavior/contract

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), which throws IllegalStateException if no CryptoProvider implementation can be located via ServiceLoader on that classloader. Previously AuthzClient did not require any CryptoProvider to be present at all. Consumers that shade/repackage the authz-client jar in a way that drops or fails to merge META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider, or that load AuthzClient with a restrictive classloader, will now get a hard failure on client creation where they previously worked fine. This is a backward-incompatible behavior change that should be called out/tested explicitly.

Silent resolution of multiple CryptoProviders removes a useful safety check

Previously detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath, which caught classpath/packaging misconfigurations early and loudly. Now it silently sorts by order() and picks the highest, logging the ignored providers only at debug level (which is typically filtered out in production). Worse, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order()==200, so if two of these full-featured providers accidentally end up on the same classpath (e.g. a packaging mistake bundling both the default and elytron crypto modules), the chosen provider now depends on ServiceLoader iteration order (effectively classpath/jar ordering), which is not guaranteed to be stable across environments. This can silently select the wrong crypto backend instead of failing fast, which is a real risk for a security-sensitive subsystem.

Single shared EC key reused for ES256/ES384/ES512 tests does not match expected curve sizes

The test generates a single EC key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (no curve specified, defaulting typically to a 256-bit curve) and reuses it for testES256, testES384 and testES512. For ES384 and ES512, the real signature r/s values will actually be ~32 bytes (P-256 sized), not the 48/66 bytes implied by algorithm.getSignatureLength(). The round-trip only passes because integerToBytes() zero-pads/truncates to the expected length, masking the fact that the conversion logic is never exercised with genuinely 384-bit or 521-bit curve signatures. This reduces the test's value and could hide bugs that only manifest with real P-384/P-521 keys.

readInteger/readLength does not guard against indefinite-length (0x80) DER encoding producing negative array size

readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80) but this is not validated by callers. In readInteger(), `int length = readLength();` followed by `byte[] bytes = read(length);` will attempt `new byte[-1]` if length is -1, throwing an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException instead of a handled IOException. Since this decoder parses externally supplied DER-encoded signature bytes (attacker-influenced JWT/token signatures), malformed input can trigger an unexpected unchecked exception instead of a predictable IOException, which callers may not be prepared to catch.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Role/Client/Group removal cleanup gated only by legacy (V1) feature flag, not V2

The provider event listener that disables permissions on RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent is now wrapped in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`, checking only the legacy V1 feature. When only ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled (V1 disabled), this block never executes, so no cleanup/disable logic runs at all when a client, role, or group is removed under the V2 fine-grained authorization model. Since the corresponding V2 permission classes (e.g. ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled) throw UnsupportedOperationException, this avoids a crash, but it also means there is no equivalent cleanup path for V2 schema data (e.g. orphaned per-client/per-user resources or policies referencing a removed client, role, or group), risking stale/orphaned authorization data over time.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission only matches the 'all-clients' meta-resource, not individual client resources

getClientsWithPermission() calls resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) to find resources of type 'Clients'. However, the per-client resources created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() (resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())) never call resource.setType(...); only the single meta resource representing the whole resource type ('Clients') gets its type set during AdminPermissionsSchema.init(). As a result, findByType will only ever return that one meta resource, so getClientsWithPermission() cannot discover individual per-client grants and would at best add the literal resource name 'Clients' (not an actual client id) to the result set when an 'all clients' permission is granted. Any caller relying on this method to filter/list clients a caller has permission for (e.g. client listing endpoints) will silently miss clients granted via individual resource permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Potential NullPointerException when the 'all-clients' meta resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when the per-client resource is null, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) to get the 'all-clients' resource, then immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking whether that call returned null. getResourceTypeResource() returns null if the resourceType is unknown or if resourceStore.findByName() doesn't find the meta resource (e.g. the admin-permissions client's resource server hasn't been fully initialized). In that case findByResource is invoked with a null resource, which is likely to throw a NullPointerException instead of gracefully denying the permission.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
New MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope added to Clients schema has no test coverage

AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS now includes the MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope (used by ClientPermissionsV2.canMapClientScopeRoles), but PermissionClientTest only imports and exercises MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE (see testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient). There is no test validating that granting/denying MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE actually controls the ability to map client-scope roles for a client, leaving this new capability unverified.

Several ClientPermissionEvaluator methods unconditionally throw UnsupportedOperationException in V2

canExchangeTo, exchangeToPermission, mapRolesPermission, mapRolesClientScopePermission, mapRolesCompositePermission, managePermission, configurePermission, viewPermission, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, and getPermissions are all overridden to throw UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported in V2'). If any existing call site (e.g. token exchange flow calling canExchangeTo, or admin console code retrieving a client's permission map via getPermissions/resource) is invoked while ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, this will propagate as an unchecked RuntimeException resulting in a 500 Internal Server Error instead of a controlled 403/empty response, rather than failing gracefully.

getResourceName() was not updated to handle the new CLIENTS resource type

getResourceName() has special-case handling that maps a 'Users' resource to a friendly display ('All users' for the all-resource meta entry, or the username for a specific user resource). No equivalent branch was added for the new CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE/CLIENTS resource type introduced by this PR. For permissions scoped to 'Clients' it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set when the resource is created in getOrCreateResource() (displayName isn't populated there), and there's no 'All clients' label for the all-resource meta entry either. This results in blank/unclear resource names being shown for Client-type permissions (e.g. in the admin console or REST responses), unlike the equivalent User-type permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE value changed from 4 to 3, repurposing 4 for FEATURE_DISABLED

The constant RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE is changed from 4 to 3, and the previously-used value 4 is now repurposed to mean FEATURE_DISABLED. Anyone who has already scripted around the previous exit-code contract (where 4 meant 'recreate upgrade required') will now get a different, incompatible meaning for the same exit code. Even though the docs for this preview tool already described code 3 for recreate-required (meaning the running implementation and docs were previously inconsistent), this PR silently changes the runtime behavior of an already-usable CLI command. Given the documentation explicitly instructs consumers to rely on the exit code contract ('they should rely only on the exit code of the check command'), this is a user-facing behavioral change that should be called out clearly in release notes / changelog, not just silently fixed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION block wording overstates scope of failure

The CAUTION note states 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail,' which reads as if the entire Operator stops working without this feature. Based on the accompanying NOTE and the UpgradeTest.java changes (where the default/null update-strategy path does not enable the rolling-updates feature and still works, mimicking old behavior), the feature is only required when the update.strategy field is explicitly configured. The CAUTION text should clarify that only configuring spec.update.strategy requires the feature, to avoid readers believing they must always enable the preview feature flag for the Operator to function at all.

Feature key hardcoded as string literal instead of using the Feature enum

printFeatureDisabled() hardcodes the string 'rolling-updates' in the error message instead of referencing Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey(). If the feature's enum name or generated key is ever changed, this message will silently become inconsistent with the actual required feature flag, misleading users on how to enable the feature.

testFeatureNotEnabled does not assert the exit code

The new test testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the printed error message but never verifies that the command exits with CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED (4), which is the actual contract this PR introduces/relies on (also documented in update-compatibility.adoc). Without an exit-code assertion, a regression that changes or removes the picocli.exit(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED) call in UpdateCompatibilityCheck/UpdateCompatibilityMetadata would not be caught by this test.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() for groups treats VIEW permission as MANAGE permission

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (no-arg), when the admin role check fails, the code calls `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` instead of checking only the MANAGE scope. This means any admin who was granted only a VIEW permission on the 'all-groups' (or an individual group that falls back to the all-groups resource) will pass `canManage()`. This method gates mutating operations such as `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup()` (`auth.groups().requireManage()`), so a user with read-only access to groups can create/manage groups - a privilege escalation. Compare with `GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(GroupModel group)` which correctly checks only `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE`, and with `UserPermissionEvaluator#canManage()`'s javadoc which only mentions MANAGE. The added javadoc on `GroupPermissionEvaluator#canManage()` documents this VIEW/MANAGE behavior as intentional, which is misleading and should be corrected along with the implementation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses Resource's internal id instead of the group id

In `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`, the iteration does `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, groupResource -> { if (hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)) { granted.add(groupResource.getId()); } })`. However, per `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`/`resolveGroup`, the actual group id is stored as the resource's *name*, not its (randomly generated) *id*. `hasPermission(groupId, ...)` subsequently does `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so passing `groupResource.getId()` will never find the per-group resource and will always fall back to the 'all-groups' schema resource evaluation. Consequently: (1) per-group permissions are effectively ignored for this method, with results only reflecting whether an 'all-groups' permission exists for any of the requested scopes, and (2) the returned Set contains internal resource IDs rather than real group IDs. These IDs are used verbatim by callers such as `UsersResource.getUsersCount(realm, search, groupIds)` and session attribute `UserModel.GROUPS`, so downstream filtering by group membership is broken (counts/filters will not match real groups). It should use `groupResource.getName()` both for the permission check and for the value added to the result set.

false_positives.candidate:
No negative test verifying VIEW-only permission does not grant manage capability

`testManageAllGroups()` only verifies that granting the MANAGE scope allows group creation/management; there is no test asserting that granting only the VIEW scope at the all-groups (or per-group) level does NOT allow create/update/delete operations. Such a test would have caught the bug in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() where VIEW permission is mistakenly treated as sufficient for MANAGE-gated operations like creating top-level groups.

Removed global-view short-circuit causes a per-group authorization evaluation

Previously `canViewGlobal = groupsEvaluator.canView()` was computed once and used as `g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g)`, so when the caller has a blanket view permission, no further per-group evaluation was needed. The change to `stream.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)` removes this optimization: for FGAP V2 (`GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel)`), each call performs a fresh policy-engine evaluation (`hasPermission(group.getId(), VIEW, MANAGE)`) per group instead of reusing a single global result, which can significantly degrade performance for realms with many groups when the admin's visibility is granted at the all-groups level rather than via a role.

Removed global-view short-circuit in getSubGroups causes a per-group authorization evaluation

Similar to GroupsResource.getGroups, `getSubGroups` previously hoisted `canViewGlobal = auth.groups().canView()` out of the filter loop (`g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g)`), but now uses `.filter(auth.groups()::canView)` directly. Under FGAP V2, this forces a separate policy evaluation for every subgroup instead of computing the global permission once, which is a performance regression for groups with many subgroups when the caller only holds a blanket (all-groups) view permission rather than a role.

Tests only exercise a single group, hiding getGroupIdsWithViewPermission correctness issues

The membership-based tests (testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers / testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers) only create a single group with a single permission. Because `GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` incorrectly falls back to an 'all-groups' evaluation for every resource it iterates (see separate finding), a scenario with multiple groups - one with a scoped permission and one without - would be needed to detect that the method does not correctly restrict visibility to only the permitted group, and that the returned IDs are not valid group IDs usable by callers such as `getUsersCount`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.

The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Fragile string-based resolution of the English reference file

The English counterpart file is located by doing a plain string replace on the absolute path (`resources-community`→`resources`, then `_<locale>.properties`→`_en.properties`). This assumes every verified properties file lives in a `resources`/`resources-community` theme tree with a sibling `_en.properties` file following exactly this naming convention. If a file doesn't match this pattern (e.g. is not itself under one of these two trees, has a differently-formed locale suffix, or has no English counterpart at all), `new FileInputStream(englishFile)` will throw `FileNotFoundException`, which is wrapped in a `RuntimeException` (see line 78-79) instead of a clear Maven error. This makes the verifier brittle to any directory/naming variation and produces a confusing stack trace rather than an actionable build failure.

Hard-coded, non-extensible whitelist for MessageFormat choice/placeholder exceptions

normalizeValue() special-cases only four specific keys (`templateHelp`, `optimizeLookupHelp`, keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit`, and `error-invalid-multivalued-size`) to strip angle-bracket placeholders or MessageFormat `{n,choice,...}` syntax that would otherwise be mistaken for HTML by the sanitizer. Any future message key that introduces similar `{n,choice,...}` syntax or literal `<...>` placeholder text (as several locale files in this very PR needed, e.g. `error-invalid-multivalued-size` in multiple languages) will not be covered by this list and will cause false 'Illegal HTML' failures until someone manually extends this hard-coded list. There is no generic handling of MessageFormat choice syntax across all keys, only for the enumerated ones.

New dependency versions hard-coded instead of using property placeholders

The newly added `owasp-java-html-sanitizer` (20240325.1) and `commons-text` (1.13.0) dependencies have their versions hard-coded inline, while every other dependency in this pom (maven-plugin-api, maven-plugin-tools, etc.) uses a `<properties>`-defined version variable. This is inconsistent with the existing convention in the file and makes future version bumps/dependency management (e.g. via a BOM) harder to track centrally.

No positive-path tests for the new HTML/anchor sanitizer All four new/updated tests (`verifyIllegalHtmlTagDetected`, `verifyNoHtmlAllowed`, `verifyNoChangedAnchors`, and the duplicate-key test) only assert that violations are correctly detected. There is no test confirming that a translation containing legitimate HTML matching the English source (e.g. matching ``/``/`

` tags in both English and translation) passes verification without any findings. Given the complexity of the anchor-matching and choice-format normalization logic in `VerifyMessageProperties`, lacking a 'happy path' regression test risks silently breaking valid translations in the future without any test failing.

Unchecked RuntimeException bypasses the MojoExecutionException contract

verify() declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and only catches `IOException` around the call to `verifySafeHtml()`. However, `verifySafeHtml()` wraps any IOException it encounters (e.g. missing English file, line 70 and 78-79) in an unchecked `RuntimeException`, which is not caught by the `catch (IOException e)` in `verify()`. As a result, any failure while reading the referenced English file propagates out of `verify()` as a raw RuntimeException, bypassing the plugin's intended error-reporting path and surfacing as an unhandled exception in the Maven build instead of a clean, actionable error message.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor validates grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId for null

Under concurrent requests triggering the same lazy-resolution path, one thread could observe one map updated but not the other, leading to a transient inconsistency between the two maps. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (line 335-338) and terminate() (line 340-342) both call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently stops all worker threads and shuts down all underlying queue.Queue objects. However, queue_pool is the SAME object that lives on ResultsStrategyFactory (created once in __init__, see result_consumer.py) and is intended to persist across the whole lifetime of the consumer process - it is only supposed to be torn down once via ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(). In Arroyo, create_with_partitions() is invoked on every partition assignment change (rebalance), and the previous strategy instance's close()/join() are called first. That means on the very first rebalance, the shared queue_pool's workers/queues are shut down for good, while factory.queue_pool still points at this now-dead pool. The next strategy created by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker() reuses this dead queue_pool. When submit() then calls work_queue.put(work_item) on a queue that has been shut down, queue.ShutDown is raised, caught by the broad except Exception in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), which force-marks the offset as added+completed without ever having it processed. The net effect: after the first rebalance, uptime results stop being processed entirely while Kafka offsets keep advancing normally (silent data loss, no lag/alerting signal).

Sequential worker joins in shutdown() can block for minutes

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 231-243) iterates over all workers sequentially and calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) for each one. With the default num_queues=20, if several workers are slow to exit (e.g. stuck in a long-running result_processor call), the overall shutdown can block for up to num_queues * 5 seconds (100s by default) before returning. Combined with the fact that this shutdown path is invoked from strategy close()/terminate() on every rebalance (see related finding), this can cause the whole consumer to stall far beyond typical graceful-shutdown/rebalance timeouts, risking forced kills by orchestration and loss of the ability to commit final offsets.

FixedQueuePool creates each worker queue as queue.Queue() with no maxsize (line 185), yet the class docstring (around line 253, 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up') and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring both claim backpressure is provided. Because the queues are unbounded, a single slow/stuck group can cause its queue to grow without limit while submit() keeps accepting and enqueuing new items, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the advertised backpressure. This undermines the stated goal of isolating a slow item's impact.

Relies on Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API

queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added in Python 3.13. OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132-133, 142-143) and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) (line 238) to unblock worker threads. If the project's supported/runtime Python version is older than 3.13, q.shutdown() will raise AttributeError (caught and merely logged at line 238-240), but the workers will then never receive a ShutDown signal and will remain blocked forever on work_queue.get(), so worker.join(timeout=5.0) will always time out without the thread actually stopping. This silently defeats the entire graceful-shutdown mechanism on any Python version prior to 3.13.

join(timeout) ignores the caller-supplied timeout

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) (lines 344-345) ignores the timeout parameter entirely and always calls self.close(), which itself uses hardcoded internal timeouts (5.0s for the commit thread plus up to 5.0s per worker in queue_pool.shutdown()). Callers (e.g. Arroyo's StreamProcessor, which is configured with join_timeout) expect join() to respect the requested deadline for bounding shutdown time; ignoring it can make the strategy's shutdown take substantially longer than what was configured, breaking the ProcessingStrategy contract.

get_committable_offsets does an O(n) scan under a lock on every tick, scaling with backlog size

get_committable_offsets() (lines 67-98) iterates offset-by-offset from last_committed+1 to max_offset while holding the per-partition lock, and this runs every second from the commit loop. If one group backlogs its queue (the exact scenario this PR intends to tolerate), the gap between last_committed and max_offset for that partition grows large, making this scan increasingly expensive and holding the partition lock longer each tick - which blocks add_offset()/complete_offset() calls from worker threads processing unrelated groups on the same partition, partially reintroducing the contention the queue-based design was meant to avoid.

No test exercises strategy close()/recreate across a simulated rebalance

All of the new thread-queue-parallel tests (test_thread_queue_parallel, test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order, etc.) build a single strategy via factory.create_with_partitions() and only ever call factory.shutdown() at the end; none of them call consumer.close() (or terminate()) and then call factory.create_with_partitions() again to simulate a Kafka rebalance and continue processing more messages. This is exactly the scenario where the shared FixedQueuePool gets torn down by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() (see related finding), so the test suite does not catch that the thread-queue-parallel mode becomes non-functional after the first rebalance.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the grant shortcut is supposed to occupy characters at index 4-5 of the 6-char context prefix (2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type), but the code extracts `items[0].substring(3, 5)` instead of `substring(4, 6)`, picking the wrong characters. On top of that, the boolean logic is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (no match) when the (wrong) substring equals the expected shortcut, and otherwise falls through to only check the UUID portion. Combining the wrong substring with the inverted condition means the comparison practically never triggers a failure based on the expected grant shortcut — the matcher effectively validates only the UUID suffix and silently ignores the grant-type encoding it claims to check. All the `expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` assertions that rely on `isAccessTokenId(...)` therefore do not actually verify that the correct grant-type shortcut was encoded into the access token id, defeating the purpose of this test helper and of the related integration tests.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies both issues in the golden comment: the grant shortcut should use substring(4, 6), and equality should indicate a match combined with UUID validation rather than return false.

false_positives.candidate:
Access token id format changed from plain UUID to a prefixed, colon-delimited string

`initToken()` previously set the token id (`jti`) to a plain UUID via `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()`. Now the id is produced by `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)`, which prepends a 6-character context prefix and a colon (e.g. `onrtac:1f65761e-...`) before the UUID. This is a visible change to the structure/length of the standard `jti` claim for every access token issued going forward. Any external system, client library, logging/SIEM tooling, or custom Keycloak extension that parses or validates the access token id as a bare UUID (length 36, dash positions, etc.) will break. The PR does not appear to document this as a breaking change or provide an opt-out/compatibility mode for consumers relying on the previous format.

Removal of public copy constructor breaks binary/source compatibility for OAuth2GrantType.Context

The previously public `Context(Context context)` copy constructor has been removed entirely from `OAuth2GrantType.Context`, which lives in `server-spi-private` and is part of the SPI surface used by custom/extension `OAuth2GrantType` implementations. Any third-party code (or future in-tree code) that relied on this copy constructor to clone/extend a `Context` instance will fail to compile after this change. Since this is an SPI-facing class, its public constructors should be treated as part of the public contract and removing one without deprecation is a breaking API change.

Non-atomic two-map update when lazily resolving unknown grant shortcuts

`getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` update the two `ConcurrentHashMap`s (`grantsByShortcuts` and `grantsToShortcuts`) with separate, non-atomic `put` calls when a grant type is not found in the initially populated maps (e.g., a provider deployed after `postInit`). Under concurrent requests triggering the same lazy-resolution path, one thread could observe one map updated but not the other, leading to a transient inconsistency between the two maps. While the code recovers on subsequent calls, this is a minor race that could be avoided by computing both updates together (e.g., with `computeIfAbsent` or a lock) rather than as two sequential, independently-visible writes.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes stored unhashed when delegated to a UserStorageProvider

createRecoveryCodesCredential() builds the UserCredentialModel passed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential() from the raw, un-hashed `generatedCodes` list (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes), line 119/123) and hands that straight to the federated storage provider's updateCredential(). This bypasses the hashing mechanism that RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode()/verifyRecoveryCodeInput() implement for the local (DB) path, where only hashed codes are ever persisted via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel. If a UserStorageProvider accepts the credential (returns true), the plaintext one-time recovery codes end up stored verbatim in the external store, unlike the hashed representation used for Keycloak's own storage. This is a security regression: anyone with read access to the external store (or its logs/backups) can recover valid one-time codes, defeating the purpose of hashing recovery codes in the first place.

Javadoc does not document the plaintext-vs-hashed storage discrepancy

The method's Javadoc ("Create RecoveryCodes credential either in userStorage or local storage") gives no indication that the two branches store fundamentally different representations: the user-storage branch persists raw, unhashed codes while the local-storage fallback persists hashed codes via credentialModel. This is a crucial behavioral detail for anyone implementing or reviewing a custom UserStorageProvider for this credential type, and its omission can easily lead integrators to assume codes are hashed everywhere.

Reference test provider validates recovery codes by plaintext comparison, codifying insecure pattern

isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE deserializes the stored credential data and compares the raw input challenge response directly against the stored list with `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. Since this reference/test implementation (meant to illustrate correct SPI usage) stores and compares plaintext codes, it reinforces the plaintext-storage pattern introduced in CredentialHelper rather than demonstrating a secure implementation (e.g., hashing the codes itself before persisting), which real third-party storage implementers may copy.

getCredentials() returns a live mutable reference to internal state

credentialModels.add(myUser.getOtp()) adds the stored CredentialModel object directly (same reference held in the shared `users` map) instead of a defensive copy. Any caller that mutates the returned CredentialModel (e.g., through generic credential-management code that edits fields in place) would silently corrupt the provider's internal state for that user, since there is no copy-on-read protection. The same applies to the newly added recoveryCodes exposure path.

New recovery-codes test does not verify stored data format/security, only functional login

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin() only exercises the happy-path (setup codes, log in with one). It never asserts what is actually persisted in the federated storage (e.g., whether codes are stored hashed or in plaintext), nor does it cover negative cases such as entering an invalid/used code, disabling the credential through admin/account REST, or re-authenticating after all codes are consumed when backed by a UserStorageProvider. Given the security-sensitive change to how/where codes are stored (see CredentialHelper), a test asserting the persisted representation would be valuable to catch regressions like plaintext storage.

Previously detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath, which caught classpath/packaging misconfigurations early and loudly. Now it silently sorts by order() and picks the highest, logging the ignored providers only at debug level (which is typically filtered out in production). Worse, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order()==200, so if two of these full-featured providers accidentally end up on the same classpath (e.g. a packaging mistake bundling both the default and elytron crypto modules), the chosen provider now depends on ServiceLoader iteration order (effectively classpath/jar ordering), which is not guaranteed to be stable across environments. This can silently select the wrong crypto backend instead of failing fast, which is a real risk for a security-sensitive subsystem.

The test generates a single EC key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (no curve specified, defaulting typically to a 256-bit curve) and reuses it for testES256, testES384 and testES512. For ES384 and ES512, the real signature r/s values will actually be ~32 bytes (P-256 sized), not the 48/66 bytes implied by algorithm.getSignatureLength(). The round-trip only passes because integerToBytes() zero-pads/truncates to the expected length, masking the fact that the conversion logic is never exercised with genuinely 384-bit or 521-bit curve signatures. This reduces the test's value and could hide bugs that only manifest with real P-384/P-521 keys.

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), which throws IllegalStateException if no CryptoProvider implementation can be located via ServiceLoader on that classloader. Previously AuthzClient did not require any CryptoProvider to be present at all. Consumers that shade/repackage the authz-client jar in a way that drops or fails to merge META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider, or that load AuthzClient with a restrictive classloader, will now get a hard failure on client creation where they previously worked fine. This is a backward-incompatible behavior change that should be called out/tested explicitly.

In readInteger(), `int length = readLength();` followed by `byte[] bytes = read(length);` will attempt `new byte[-1]` if length is -1, throwing an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException instead of a handled IOException. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the full-function lock in BuildIndex allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu.Lock() for its entire duration, which incidentally serialized all builds, including two concurrent calls for the same NamespacedResource key. The new code only takes cacheMu when writing the final result into b.cache (near the end of the function), so two goroutines can now run BuildIndex concurrently for the same key (this is a real possibility because searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex in search.go checks GetIndex and calls build() without any per-key lock, a gap already flagged by a TODO comment in that file). Concurrent builds for the same key can both call bleve.New()/bleve.NewMemOnly() and write documents independently, then race to overwrite b.cache[key], silently discarding one index's work or, for file-backed indexes sharing the same directory, causing on-disk index corruption/contention.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: moving cacheMu from a full-function lock to only the final cache assignment allows concurrent goroutines to build duplicate expensive indexes for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

TotalDocs() reads the cache map without holding cacheMu

Because real concurrent map writes now happen during startup/runtime, a concurrent call to TotalDocs() (e.g. from a metrics scrape or another caller) racing with a BuildIndex write to the same map can trigger Go's 'concurrent map read and map write' fatal error, crashing the process. This hazard existed before but is made materially worse by the increased real concurrency this PR introduces for cache writes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while BuildIndex may write concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic. false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer now blocks synchronously on full index build during startup

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) directly in the constructor, which in turn calls searchSupport.init(), which builds the search index for every namespace returned by GetResourceStats before returning. Previously this cost was paid lazily inside the first gRPC call (with its own deadline); now it is paid unconditionally at construction time with no timeout. If NewResourceServer is invoked anywhere besides the dedicated storage-server module (e.g. during normal Grafana app-server bootstrap for unified storage), overall process startup can block for an arbitrarily long time while every namespace's index is built, and any failure during that build (e.g. a transient DB error) now causes server construction itself to fail outright rather than only a particular RPC. The PR description explicitly raises this as an open question ('What could this break?') but does not resolve it — there is no bound on index-build time nor any fallback/async option.

Stop() no longer gates any RPC after shutdown

Previously every RPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) called s.Init(ctx) first; since Init used sync.Once, after Stop() set s.initErr to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", those calls to Init(ctx) would surface that error to callers. This PR removes the s.Init(ctx) calls from all RPC handlers, so the initErr set in Stop() is now write-only dead state — no code path reads it anymore. As a result, after Stop() is called, in-flight or new RPCs will no longer get a clean 'service is stopping/stopped' error; they will instead proceed against a server whose background context (s.ctx) has already been cancelled (e.g. broadcaster/watch loops torn down), leading to inconsistent or silent failures instead of a clear error to the caller.

Postgres integration test disabled instead of fixed, losing coverage for the exact startup-init change

This PR adds a skip for dbType == "postgres" in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer with only the comment 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' No root cause or follow-up ticket is referenced. Since this PR's core change is moving unified-storage initialization into server startup (which can now block or fail at NewResourceServer time), disabling exactly the integration test that exercises a real storage-server startup against postgres removes the only regression coverage for that scenario, rather than investigating why it fails under the new init-at-startup behavior.

false_positives.candidate:
close()/terminate() tear down the shared, persistent FixedQueuePool, breaking processing after any rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (line 335-338) and terminate() (line 340-342) both call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently stops all worker threads and shuts down all underlying queue.Queue objects. However, queue_pool is the SAME object that lives on ResultsStrategyFactory (created once in __init__, see result_consumer.py) and is intended to persist across the whole lifetime of the consumer process - it is only supposed to be torn down once via ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(). In Arroyo, create_with_partitions() is invoked on every partition assignment change (rebalance), and the previous strategy instance's close()/join() are called first. That means on the very first rebalance, the shared queue_pool's workers/queues are shut down for good, while factory.queue_pool still points at this now-dead pool. The next strategy created by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker() reuses this dead queue_pool. When submit() then calls work_queue.put(work_item) on a queue that has been shut down, queue.ShutDown is raised, caught by the broad except Exception in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), which force-marks the offset as added+completed without ever having it processed. The net effect: after the first rebalance, uptime results stop being processed entirely while Kafka offsets keep advancing normally (silent data loss, no lag/alerting signal).

Sequential worker joins in shutdown() can block for minutes

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 231-243) iterates over all workers sequentially and calls worker.join(timeout=5.0) for each one. With the default num_queues=20, if several workers are slow to exit (e.g. stuck in a long-running result_processor call), the overall shutdown can block for up to num_queues * 5 seconds (100s by default) before returning. Combined with the fact that this shutdown path is invoked from strategy close()/terminate() on every rebalance (see related finding), this can cause the whole consumer to stall far beyond typical graceful-shutdown/rebalance timeouts, risking forced kills by orchestration and loss of the ability to commit final offsets.

Queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure guarantee

FixedQueuePool creates each worker queue as queue.Queue() with no maxsize (line 185), yet the class docstring (around line 253, 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up') and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring both claim backpressure is provided. Because the queues are unbounded, a single slow/stuck group can cause its queue to grow without limit while submit() keeps accepting and enqueuing new items, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the advertised backpressure. This undermines the stated goal of isolating a slow item's impact.

Relies on Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API

queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added in Python 3.13. OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132-133, 142-143) and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) (line 238) to unblock worker threads. If the project's supported/runtime Python version is older than 3.13, q.shutdown() will raise AttributeError (caught and merely logged at line 238-240), but the workers will then never receive a ShutDown signal and will remain blocked forever on work_queue.get(), so worker.join(timeout=5.0) will always time out without the thread actually stopping. This silently defeats the entire graceful-shutdown mechanism on any Python version prior to 3.13.

join(timeout) ignores the caller-supplied timeout

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) (lines 344-345) ignores the timeout parameter entirely and always calls self.close(), which itself uses hardcoded internal timeouts (5.0s for the commit thread plus up to 5.0s per worker in queue_pool.shutdown()). Callers (e.g. Arroyo's StreamProcessor, which is configured with join_timeout) expect join() to respect the requested deadline for bounding shutdown time; ignoring it can make the strategy's shutdown take substantially longer than what was configured, breaking the ProcessingStrategy contract.

get_committable_offsets does an O(n) scan under a lock on every tick, scaling with backlog size

get_committable_offsets() (lines 67-98) iterates offset-by-offset from last_committed+1 to max_offset while holding the per-partition lock, and this runs every second from the commit loop. If one group backlogs its queue (the exact scenario this PR intends to tolerate), the gap between last_committed and max_offset for that partition grows large, making this scan increasingly expensive and holding the partition lock longer each tick - which blocks add_offset()/complete_offset() calls from worker threads processing unrelated groups on the same partition, partially reintroducing the contention the queue-based design was meant to avoid.

No test exercises strategy close()/recreate across a simulated rebalance

All of the new thread-queue-parallel tests (test_thread_queue_parallel, test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order, etc.) build a single strategy via factory.create_with_partitions() and only ever call factory.shutdown() at the end; none of them call consumer.close() (or terminate()) and then call factory.create_with_partitions() again to simulate a Kafka rebalance and continue processing more messages. This is exactly the scenario where the shared FixedQueuePool gets torn down by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() (see related finding), so the test suite does not catch that the thread-queue-parallel mode becomes non-functional after the first rebalance.

Since this is an SPI-facing class, its public constructors should be treated as part of the public contract and removing one without deprecation is a breaking API change.

While the code recovers on subsequent calls, this is a minor race that could be avoided by computing both updates together (e.g., with `computeIfAbsent` or a lock) rather than as two sequential, independently-visible writes.

However, queue_pool is the SAME object that lives on ResultsStrategyFactory (created once in __init__, see result_consumer.py) and is intended to persist across the whole lifetime of the consumer process - it is only supposed to be torn down once via ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(). In Arroyo, create_with_partitions() is invoked on every partition assignment change (rebalance), and the previous strategy instance's close()/join() are called first. Combined with the fact that this shutdown path is invoked from strategy close()/terminate() on every rebalance (see related finding), this can cause the whole consumer to stall far beyond typical graceful-shutdown/rebalance timeouts, risking forced kills by orchestration and loss of the ability to commit final offsets.

Because the queues are unbounded, a single slow/stuck group can cause its queue to grow without limit while submit() keeps accepting and enqueuing new items, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the advertised backpressure. This undermines the stated goal of isolating a slow item's impact.

queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added in Python 3.13. If the project's supported/runtime Python version is older than 3.13, q.shutdown() will raise AttributeError (caught and merely logged at line 238-240), but the workers will then never receive a ShutDown signal and will remain blocked forever on work_queue.get(), so worker.join(timeout=5.0) will always time out without the thread actually stopping. get_committable_offsets() (lines 67-98) iterates offset-by-offset from last_committed+1 to max_offset while holding the per-partition lock, and this runs every second from the commit loop. If one group backlogs its queue (the exact scenario this PR intends to tolerate), the gap between last_committed and max_offset for that partition grows large, making this scan increasingly expensive and holding the partition lock longer each tick - which blocks add_offset()/complete_offset() calls from worker threads processing unrelated groups on the same partition, partially reintroducing the contention the queue-based design was meant to avoid.

Meanwhile `has_root_span_key` is set independently as a separate boolean flag and is not affected by eviction. If the actual root span payload is evicted, `flush_segments` in buffer.py (which derives `is_segment` by comparing each remaining payload's `span_id` to the segment key) will never find a span with `is_segment=True`, even though the segment is still flushed as if it has a root span. This PR's stated purpose is 'eviction during insert' via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua when a segment exceeds 1000 spans, but no test in tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py exercises this path (e.g., inserting >1000 spans into one segment and asserting that only the most recent 1000 remain, or that a root span is preserved). true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache key can collide across distinct (name, parentFolder) pairs

userPermDenialCacheKey builds the cache key by naively concatenating userUID, action, name and parent with '_' as separator: namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. Because resource UIDs (name/parentFolder) can themselves legally contain underscores, two different requests can produce the same concatenated string, e.g. name="ab_cd", parent="ef" and name="ab", parent="cd_ef" both yield "..._ab_cd_ef". When this happens, a denial cached for one (name, parent) pair will be served for an unrelated resource, causing an incorrect 'denied' result to be returned for a resource the caller actually has access to (or, if the collision is reversed, the opposite type of mistake could occur with other callers sharing the key space). This is a correctness/security risk introduced by the new denial cache, since the previous caches never combined multiple variable-length, potentially-overlapping fields into one key this way.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug in userPermDenialCacheKey: underscore-separated concatenation of variable fields can produce ambiguous or colliding keys when fields contain underscores or delimiters, leading to incorrect denial-cache hits and permission decisions.

The denial-cache key uses checkReq.UserUID directly (the raw identifier parsed from the Subject string), whereas every other cache in this service (idCache, permCache, teamCache, basicRoleCache) is keyed on the canonical identifier returned by GetUserIdentifiers (userIdentifiers.UID), which can resolve either a numeric ID or a UID to the same canonical value. If different callers pass the subject using different formats (numeric internal ID vs. UID) for the same user, the denial cache will never be shared between them, defeating the purpose of the cache and creating inconsistent caching behavior between the positive permission cache and the new denial cache.

After a Check() call determines (via a fresh DB query) that a user is not allowed to access a resource, the result is cached for shortCacheTTL (30s) via permDenialCache.Set. If the user is subsequently granted access to that exact resource (e.g., permission is shared, or role changed) within that 30s window, Check() will short-circuit on the denial cache (lines 117-121) and return Allowed=false without consulting the DB, even though the user now has permission. This is the same category of staleness bug the PR is trying to fix for newly-created resources (stale positive cache), but now reintroduced via the new negative cache for recently-denied lookups.

In Check(), when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cache hit but checkPermission on the cached permissions evaluates to false, execution falls through past the `if err == nil { ... }` block and records `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...)` (line 137), labeling this as a cache miss even though the cache was actually hit (just didn't contain the requested permission). This produces misleading cache-hit-ratio metrics for operators monitoring cache effectiveness.

Denial-cache short-circuit test doesn't verify the cache path was actually used

The subtest 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' sets s.permDenialCache and expects resp.Allowed == false, but it never asserts that the fallback store/identity lookups were skipped (e.g. via store.calls == 0). Since the default fakeStore used by setupService() returns no permissions anyway, the test would still pass with the same expected result even if the denial-cache short-circuit logic in Check() were removed entirely. This test therefore does not actually validate the new denial-cache behavior and would not catch a regression.

Removing client-side cache for in-proc AuthZ client increases per-call overhead

ProvideAuthZClient now wires the in-proc client with a NoopCache instead of a local cache, meaning every single Check/List call goes through the full inprocgrpc channel (including proto marshal/unmarshal through the gRPC interceptor chain) rather than being served from a short-lived client-side cache. For code paths that perform many individual Check calls in a loop (e.g., per-item authorization checks), this removes a previously-available fast path and could noticeably increase per-request latency/CPU, even though the server now has its own cache, because the gRPC call overhead itself is no longer avoided on repeated checks within the same request.

Inefficient O(n^2) string building for SQLite large-batch delete

In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size exceeding the parameter limit, the code builds the IN-clause value list by repeatedly calling fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop over all ids. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands (the added test uses 32767), this can be noticeably slow and allocate excessive memory compared to using a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a byte slice (as is already done elsewhere in this same file, e.g. in getAccessControlFilter).

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy write uses request-derived context that is likely canceled before the goroutine runs

In Create (and similarly in Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) the goroutine does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)` where the outer `ctx` is the context passed into the handler, derived from the original request context. Once the HTTP handler returns (which happens right after this goroutine is spawned, since Create/Update/Delete return immediately), the apiserver typically cancels the request context. Because the goroutine's context is a child of that same request context, it will be cancelled almost immediately, well before the intended 10s timeout, causing `d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` to fail with 'context canceled' on virtually every call. This defeats the entire purpose of Mode 3 (writing to legacy asynchronously 'as a safe measure'), since the legacy write will essentially never complete successfully. The context used in the goroutine should be detached from request cancellation (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` combined with the timeout, or a fresh background context carrying only the relevant values).

Storage Update error incorrectly recorded via recordLegacyDuration

On the error path after `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, mislabeling a unified-storage error as a legacy error. This should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`, consistent with the Delete and DeleteCollection error paths.

Async legacy writes silently drop error details, losing observability on failures

The previous (synchronous) implementation logged errors from the Legacy store calls (e.g. `log.Error(errLS, "could not delete from legacy store")`). The new async goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection only record a boolean into a duration metric and never log the actual error returned by the Legacy store call. Since these goroutines are fire-and-forget with no caller visibility, failing legacy writes become effectively invisible except through aggregate metrics, making it hard to diagnose data drift between the legacy store and unified storage.

Tests do not wait for the async legacy goroutine before asserting, making legacy-write verification unreliable

TestMode3_Create (and the Delete/Update/DeleteCollection tests) set up mock expectations on the shared `mock.Mock` for the Legacy store call, but `DualWriterMode3.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` fire the legacy write in a goroutine and return immediately. The tests assert results and move on without any synchronization (e.g. a WaitGroup or channel) to ensure the goroutine has completed. This means the tests don't actually verify the legacy write happened, and since the same `mock.Mock` instance (`m`) can continue to be accessed by a lingering goroutine after the subtest finishes, running tests with `-race` can surface data races, and leftover goroutines can interact with mocks from a subsequent subtest case.

Each split sub-request will then execute with a baked-in range window from the full request instead of the correct per-chunk window, producing wrong/duplicated aggregation results for any query using $__range. This directly contradicts the rationale documented in the adjacent comment and is a data-correctness regression introduced by moving interpolation to the top of the pipeline.

The test suite only exercises this with a trivial mock replace() that happens to be idempotent, so it does not actually validate correctness of double interpolation against the real datasource implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locale translation files are only force-loaded within web requests

I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! (added in set_locale) is the only place that forces the whole fallback chain (current locale, site default locale, :en) to be loaded via I18n.ensure_loaded!. The lazy-loading patch in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb only loads the currently-active I18n.locale on a translate() call (load_locale(config.locale)), not the fallback locales. Any code path that calls I18n.t outside of ApplicationController#set_locale — background jobs, Sidekiq workers, ActionMailer deliveries, rake tasks, console sessions — will never call ensure_loaded!, so when a translation is missing for the active locale, the fallback lookup for e.g. :en can silently fail (return nil / raise MissingTranslationData) even though the English translation file exists on disk, because that locale's YAML was never actually loaded into the backend. This can produce missing/blank translations specifically in background contexts where fallback behavior is most needed.

FallbackLocaleList#[] recomputes and hits SiteSetting on every call instead of memoizing

FallbackLocaleList overrides Hash#[] to always compute [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact on every invocation rather than storing/memoizing the result in the underlying Hash. Since I18n's Fallbacks backend module calls I18n.fallbacks[locale] on essentially every translate() call (not just on a miss), this means SiteSetting.default_locale is invoked repeatedly on the hot translation path instead of once per locale, adding avoidable overhead compared to the stock I18n::Locale::Fallbacks implementation, which memoizes per-locale fallback chains in the hash itself.

FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but never populates the underlying hash store

FallbackLocaleList < Hash entirely overrides [] without ever calling super or storing values via []=/store, so the object itself remains an empty Hash. Any code that treats I18n.fallbacks as an actual Hash (e.g. enumerating via each/keys/to_a, or gems/tools that introspect configured fallback mappings) will see an empty collection instead of real data, even though direct [] lookups work correctly. This is fragile and can break downstream code that reasonably assumes I18n.fallbacks is a real, iterable Hash.

No tests added for new fallback locale behavior

This PR introduces non-trivial new behavior (FallbackLocaleList, I18n.ensure_loaded!, and the controller's forced pre-loading of the fallback chain) but adds no specs verifying that translations correctly fall back to the site default locale or to :en, nor that ensure_loaded! actually loads the required locale files. Given the subtlety of the lazy-loading/fallback interaction (see related finding about non-web contexts), this feature needs direct test coverage to avoid silent regressions.

I18n fallbacks now enabled globally instead of only in production/profile/cloud66 environments

Previously config.i18n.fallbacks = true was only set in config/environments/production.rb, profile.rb, and config/cloud/cloud66/files/production.rb. This PR removes those settings and instead enables fallbacks unconditionally for every environment via config/initializers/i18n.rb, including development and test. This is a behavior change beyond what the removed lines implied: specs or development workflows that previously relied on missing translations raising/being visibly flagged (rather than silently falling back to English) will now behave differently, which could mask incomplete translation work until it reaches a real fallback path in production anyway.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

Each app module is loaded with `import("./appname")` directly inside the object literal (e.g. `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`). These `import()` calls execute immediately when the `appStore` module is evaluated, not lazily when a given app key is actually accessed. This means all app chunks begin loading as soon as anyone imports `appStore`, exactly like the previous static-import approach, except now every consumer must `await` the property access. The PR title/description implies on-demand/code-split loading of apps, but this implementation provides no such benefit while adding overhead (every lookup becomes async) to every call site across the codebase (getCalendar, videoClient, payment helpers, etc.).

`getCalendar` was changed to be async and return `Promise<Calendar | null>`, but `getCalendarCredentials` (line 28) still calls it without `await`: `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);`. The returned `calendar` field in each credential entry is now a `Promise` instead of a resolved `Calendar` instance. Only the call site inside this same file (`getConnectedCalendars`) was updated to `await item.calendar`. Any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` elsewhere in the codebase that expects a synchronously-resolved `Calendar` object (not shown in this diff) will silently receive an unresolved Promise and break at runtime, since this is a breaking API/contract change that was not fully propagated.

getVideoAdapters resolves credentials sequentially instead of in parallel

The rewritten `getVideoAdapters` uses a `for...of` loop with `await appStore[appName]` inside, resolving each credential's app module one at a time. Previously this was a synchronous `reduce`. With multiple credentials (e.g. several video integrations configured for a booking), each dynamic import lookup is awaited sequentially rather than concurrently (e.g. via `Promise.all`), unnecessarily serializing what could be parallel async work and adding latency to booking creation/cancellation/update flows that call this function.

requestReschedule mutation does not wait for calendar/video cancellation before resolving

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` is not awaited by the surrounding `requestReschedule` mutation handler. The mutation proceeds (sending webhooks, returning to the client) without waiting for the calendar/video event deletions inside this now-async callback to complete. Since `getCalendar` is now async, each iteration performs an additional await before deleting the event, further increasing the window during which the mutation can complete and respond to the client before cancellation of the old calendar/video events has actually finished, which can cause rescheduled bookings to temporarily (or permanently, if an error occurs) leave stale calendar entries.

No tests added for the behavioral change to async app lookups

This PR changes `appStore` lookups from synchronous to asynchronous across many critical flows (calendar CRUD, video meeting creation, payment processing, booking cancellation/reschedule). No new or updated tests accompany these changes to verify that awaiting resolves correctly, that errors from unresolved/missing app keys are still handled the same way, or that the various forEach/async patterns behave as expected. Given the breadth of files touched (12 files across core booking/payment/calendar logic), this is a meaningful test gap for a change with this level of risk.
